name: Skylab 4
dispatch: Skylab 4 set an endurance record that stood for years — 84 days aloft — and became a landmark in something less expected: who gets to run a mission. Gerald Carr's crew arrived to a punishing schedule radioed up from the ground, fell behind, and eventually pushed back, taking an unscheduled rest period — NASA and the crew themselves later disputed how deliberate the stand-down was — and forcing mission control to negotiate a workload humans could actually sustain. They also captured the era's best observations of Comet Kohoutek. The flight is remembered both for its record and for asserting, for the first time clearly, that the people in orbit — not only the planners below — have a say in how a long mission is flown.
first: Longest Skylab stay — 84 days, observed Comet Kohoutek, disputed "Skylab strike" rest day
description: Carr, Gibson and Pogue — the final and longest Skylab crew, 84 days 1 hour, all-rookie. Launched 1973-11-16 14:01 UTC on Saturn IB (SA-208). Comprehensive Earth-resources and solar observation, including a full Comet Kohoutek campaign over December–January. The mission is best remembered for what NASA later called a 'Skylab mutiny' or 'strike' — a disputed account of a rest-day stand-down around day 42 after relentless ground-controller demands compressed every minute of waking time; NASA and the crew have stated no organised strike occurred, but the underlying timeline overload was real and led to permanent NASA reforms on crew time-line planning for long-duration missions. Splashed down 1974-02-08 15:17 UTC — the last Skylab splashdown. CSM-118 displayed at the National Museum of the US Air Force, Dayton OH.
